archetype.name: Fringe Contender (ball-control, QB in flux)
archetype.definition: A roughly league-average-plus team by efficiency that wins time of possession and third downs, but whose 3-2 record leans on one shootout and is now carried by a third quarterback in five weeks.

report.headline: A 3-2 team on its third quarterback, propped up by one shootout
report.take:
Chicago looks better on the standings page than on the film. The 59-37 opener at Carolina accounts for nearly the whole point differential. In the four games since, the Bears have scored 60 and allowed 59, with a 3-point dud against Minnesota and a 31-7 beating in Green Bay mixed in with two solid home wins over Philadelphia and the Jets. Net EPA ranks 12th, which fits a team that is good, not great. With winsOverExpected at 0.22, the record is honest for the point differential. The problem is that the differential flatters them.

The identity is clear. This is a run-leaning, clock-eating team (pass rate over expected -3.1) behind a line that creates space: 2.96 yards before contact ranks 4th and 4.55 a carry ranks 6th. That line plus a league-best 35.19 minutes of possession shortens games. The defense pairs that with a top-3 pressure rate and a 26% third-down conversion rate allowed, 2nd in the league. Together they explain why the Bears allow only 19.2 points a game (5th) while their defensive EPA ranks just 20th. Opponents simply don't get many snaps.

The numbers hide two things. The first is quarterback churn: Caleb Williams started weeks 1-2, Case Keenum weeks 3-4 and Tyson Bagent week 5, when the offense turned it over five times. The turnover margin has flipped from 1st in the league last year (+1.3 a game) to 30th (-1.2). The second is a defense that wins short and gets burned deep. It allows -0.207 EPA on short throws (2nd) but 1.771 on deep ones (32nd), and opposing WR1s have feasted. Last year's 11 wins also came with 2.82 wins over expected and a top turnover margin, so this franchise's recent success has been padded by luck before.

Where it heads depends on Williams' hamstring and a secondary that is already short Kyler Gordon and Anthony Johnson Jr. The turnover margin should drift back toward neutral, which helps. The third-down defense and the points-allowed rank will likely come back toward the middle, which hurts. The back half of the schedule is brutal: two Detroit games, Buffalo, Jacksonville and a finale at Minnesota. That makes this a nine-win-type team fighting for a wild card, not a division threat.

strengths.title: Pressure that wins third downs
strengths.body: Chicago gets home at the 3rd-best rate in the league and allows a 26% third-down conversion rate. Underneath throws go nowhere against it, with short-pass EPA allowed ranked 2nd. The pressure rate is the stickier half. Third-down rates this extreme usually regress, especially with LB T.J. Edwards and DE Dayo Odeyingbo banged up.

strengths.title: Run-blocking line drives ball control
strengths.body: The line creates nearly three yards before contact and helps the team lead the league in time of possession. That holds up no matter which quarterback plays, which matters for a team on its third starter. It is the most durable part of the roster. It does lose some depth with Kyle Monangai's toe injury, which puts the load on D'Andre Swift.

strengths.title: Field position from special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add about two points of EPA a game (8th). That is a quiet edge for a team built to win low-possession games. It is a modest but real contributor that doesn't depend on who plays quarterback.

trend.note: A 59-point explosion, a 3-point no-show, two clean home wins, then a five-turnover collapse in Green Bay. Three quarterbacks in five games make it hard to read any line through these results.

nextGame.headline: Road favorite with an uncertain quarterback against a top-10 defense
nextGame.body:
Atlanta is the mirror image of Chicago in style: a run-first, clock-heavy team (pass rate over expected -9, possession 5th) whose offense works on the ground and stalls through the air. That is bad news for a Bears run defense ranked 27th in rush EPA allowed. The Falcons' quick release (2.515 seconds, 31st) also blunts Chicago's best weapon, the pass rush. On the other side, Atlanta's defense ranks 7th in EPA and 3rd in success rate allowed and is stingy deep. The soft spot is WR2 production, which points to Rome Odunze. Opponents also lean pass against Atlanta more than against any other team, so the Bears may have to win through the air.

Availability drives this game on both sides. Williams is listed out, but Ben Johnson left the door open for this game, and Bagent's lone start produced five turnovers. Chicago's defense is thin: Gordon, Johnson Jr., Shemar Turner (ACL) and Keyshaun Elliott are out, and Edwards, Tyrique Stevenson and Odeyingbo are questionable. For Atlanta, Michael Penix Jr. is questionable with a rib injury after a season with three different starters, CB C.J. Henderson is questionable, and edge Za'Darius Smith is out. The roof is retractable and the early forecast is mild.

keyMatchups.title: Falcons run game vs Bears front
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta ranks 3rd in rush EPA and 2nd in yards per carry, and Chicago's defense has given lead backs about three PPR points over their norm. Missing Turner and Elliott, with Edwards questionable, the Bears could lose the possession battle they usually win.

keyMatchups.title: Odunze against Atlanta's WR2 hole
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta is strong almost everywhere in coverage, but it allows 0.51 EPA a target to WR2s (25th), and Henderson's groin is a question. Odunze is the cleanest path to explosive plays against a defense that otherwise shuts down deep balls.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game neutralizes Chicago rush
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta gets the ball out faster than almost anyone and allows the 2nd-lowest pressure rate, which mutes Chicago's top-3 pass rush. The flip side is that Atlanta's pass offense ranks 27th in EPA, so the Bears can live with short completions as long as their depleted secondary doesn't give up the deep ball.

nextGame.watch: Whether Caleb Williams starts. With Bagent, this is a coin flip on the road against a top-10 defense.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the scoring defense to give back some ground. A 20th-ranked EPA unit allowing the 5th-fewest points is being carried by time of possession and an unsustainable third-down rate, and the secondary is already depleted. The offense should be steadier once Williams returns. The run game is real, and a 30th-ranked turnover margin is more likely to improve than repeat. That is a team scoring in the low-to-mid 20s and allowing about the same.

The schedule decides the ceiling. NO, MIA and TB at home are winnable. Detroit twice, Buffalo, Jacksonville, Seattle's 2nd-ranked defense and a trip to unbeaten Minnesota are not. A finish around .500 plus a game or two keeps them in the wild-card race but well behind the Vikings.
swingFactors: Caleb Williams' hamstring and how quickly he's fully back
Health of the secondary (Gordon, Stevenson, Johnson Jr.)

bets.reason: This is the highest total of Chicago's season, yet its last four games all went under. Both teams rank top five in time of possession and lean run-heavy (PROE -3.1 and -9). Atlanta's defense is 7th in EPA, and both teams have questionable quarterbacks.

The line implies about 26 points for Chicago. The Bears have scored 3, 27, 23 and 7 since the opener, and Atlanta ranks 3rd in success rate allowed and 5th in deep EPA allowed, with Chicago's quarterback unsettled.

Net EPA has these teams nearly even (12th vs 15th), yet Chicago is laying three on the road with Williams uncertain and seven defensive contributors out or questionable. Atlanta's 3rd-ranked rushing attack also meets the Bears' 27th-ranked run defense.

confidence.note: Five games, three starting quarterbacks and one blowout skew the sample.
